text.title: Stocks slide 2% as Anthropic's record IPO fails to stem the AI selloff; S&P 500 down six straight
text.summary: US stocks fell sharply, with the S&P 500 down 2.0% (its sixth straight loss), the Nasdaq down 2.3% and the Dow down 2.2%. The VIX jumped 15.8% to 28.44. Anthropic's record debut, which had lifted futures this morning, faded as money rotated out of other AI names and China-related worries returned. Treasury yields slipped, with the 10-year at 5.05% and the 2-year at 4.76%, and the dollar edged up. Gold fell 3.1% and Bitcoin fell 2.4%, so the retreat reached the usual havens and speculative assets too. The common thread is risk-off positioning: investors are questioning AI valuations and growth, with recession worries and hot-inflation concerns in the background.
text.rates: Treasuries caught a modest haven bid: the 10-year yield fell 2 bp to 5.05% (its fourth straight decline) and the 2-year fell 4 bp to 4.76%, per WSJ as the Anthropic IPO failed to sustain risk appetite. Yields remain elevated, however. J.P. Morgan's recap shows the 10-year at 5.15% on Nov 13, and high yields raise the discount rate on long-dated earnings, which weighs most on richly valued growth stocks. The dollar index rose 0.1% to 103.94. Gold and Bitcoin both fell, so there was no clean safe haven beyond Treasuries.
text.breadth: The selling was nearly universal: all 11 sector ETFs fell. Consumer discretionary (-2.8%) and communication services (-2.7%) lagged, while energy (-0.7%), utilities (-1.2%) and staples (-1.5%) held up best. That is a defensive tilt, though those sectors still declined. The Russell 2000 fell 2.2%, in line with large caps, so small caps offered no refuge. The pattern points to broad de-risking rather than a rotation, with growth and AI-linked names bearing the heaviest pressure.
text.context: The S&P 500 is down 5.5% over five sessions and 7.0% over a month, 7.5% below its one-month high, with six straight losses. The Nasdaq is 10.6% below its recent high. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap showed the S&P 500 at 7562 and about 18.2x forward earnings as of Nov 13, so the index has since given back a meaningful part of that level. The VIX is up 52% in five days and at a one-month high.
text.takeaway: Sharp, concentrated drawdowns in a leadership theme such as AI show why diversification across sectors, styles and asset classes matters. Even so, today's declines were broad, a reminder that correlations can rise in stressed markets.
text.talk: Stocks fell about 2% today as investors kept pulling back from AI-linked shares, even after Anthropic's record IPO, while China-related concerns, cyber worries and mixed signals on growth and inflation added to the caution. Markets are volatile at the moment, and a long-term, diversified plan is designed to withstand periods like this.

drivers.t: Anthropic closed its first day at $97.17, up 17%, with a market value around $2 trillion after raising $81 billion. That wasn't enough to hold the broader tech trade up. WSJ reports that investors sold other AI holdings to fund purchases of the new listing, so the IPO acted as a funding drain rather than a catalyst. A mega-offering absorbs capital, and it also invites investors to test how much the AI buildout is worth. The Nasdaq lost 2.3% and sits 10.6% below its one-month high, and technology and communication ETFs fell 1.9% and 2.7%.

Nvidia has lost $669 billion in market value over six trading days, according to MarketWatch. Rep. Mast said Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, and members of Congress are pushing for tighter export controls after the 'Jensen Huang scandal'. AMD closed down more than 7% after a short-seller alleged its firmware turned up at a blacklisted Chinese company, which AMD denies. Micron and Broadcom gave up gains as China concerns intensified. Because Nvidia's web of ties across the AI ecosystem is so wide, a leadership or regulatory shock there tends to hit the whole supply chain.
drivers.impact: Chips hit by China, export-control risk

drivers.h: Cyber fears and 'death cross' hit banks
drivers.t: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard said third-party vendors were targeted in a cyberattack, and WSJ noted cyber fears hit financials. Bloomberg reports large US banks fell into a bearish 'death cross' technical pattern after their worst four-day run since April 2025. Vendor-level breaches matter because they raise operational and reputational risk across the whole payments chain, not just at one firm. Financials fell 1.5%, among the smaller sector declines but part of a broad retreat.

MarketWatch says recession trades are emerging even as economic data has largely held up. Meanwhile Chicago Fed President Goolsbee said all options are on the table for next month's FOMC meeting amid hot inflation, and did not push back on the possibility of a larger-than-usual move. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap noted last week's CPI rose 0.4% headline and 0.3% core. Mixed growth and inflation signals make equities harder to price, and the 2-year yield fell 4 bp to 4.76% as the risk-off tone took hold.

UnitedHealth fell again after the government signaled a crackdown on Medicare Advantage fraud and lawmakers renewed calls for Medicare for All. Policy risk to a major insurer's margins can weigh on the wider group, and health care ETFs lost 2.1%. Gap lowered full-year guidance, and WSJ noted Williams-Sonoma 'got cooked'. Consumer discretionary was the worst sector, down 2.8%.

drivers.h: Gold slides, oil steady on Mideast
drivers.t: Gold fell 3.1% to $3,624, extending a 6.7% five-day drop, and the headlines offer no direct explanation. A firmer dollar (up 0.1%, at a one-month high) tends to pressure gold, but that is a modest move for such a big decline. WTI rose 1.0% to $83.11 in a choppy session as Middle East escalation worries were offset by improving supply. The Senate blocked an Iran war resolution, and Trump said he is looking to 2027 to 'see what happens' with Iran. Oil is still down 19.8% over one month.

earnings.t: Intuit fell 10.7% after hours. The company also agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, less than a third of what it paid in 2021, offloading a slower-growth segment.
Palo Alto Networks beat expectations and agreed a $4.5 billion deal for AI startup Applied Compute, and the stock rose on the news despite the weak tape.
Gap lowered full-year guidance, reported mixed third-quarter results and named a new Athleta CEO, and it was among the after-hours movers.
